title: The tert-butyloxonium ion loses water
subtitle: A C–O bond breaks: water leaves, a carbocation forms

reactants.caption: tert-butyloxonium chloride
reactants.learnerPrompt: Draw how water leaves to give the carbocation.
hintTiers: Water is a good leaving group once it carries the positive charge. Which bond breaks?
One arrow: a bond breaks heterolytically, and both electrons go to the more electronegative atom.
One arrow: the C–O bond onto the oxygen, which leaves as water and leaves a tertiary carbocation.

misconceptions.arrowPattern: lp Cl6 -> σ Cl6-C1; σ C1-O5 -> lp O5
misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Chloride cannot reach the back of a tertiary carbon: three methyl groups are in the way. Water leaves first; chloride attacks the cation afterwards.
This carbon already has four bonds. A new bond to chloride would give it five bonds and ten electrons, which carbon can never have. A bond must break first.
The C–O bond breaks towards the positive, electronegative oxygen, not towards carbon. Water leaves with both electrons.

steps.explanationAfterStep: Oxygen takes back the pair it shared, so it is neutral again. Carbon loses a bond and its share of two electrons: three bonds, six electrons, positive. A tertiary carbocation is stabilised by its three methyl groups, which is why this ionisation is fast.

mechanismSummary: The C–O bond of the protonated alcohol breaks, and both electrons go to oxygen, which leaves as neutral water. Carbon is left with three bonds and a positive charge: the tertiary carbocation.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 5 (Organic reactions)
